Its not a legitimate security feature. The fingerprint reader should need to pass fingerprint data (or hashes) to a secondary chip (like a TPM) which holds the decryption keys. Allowing replacement of the reader itself doesn't pose any legitimate security threat.
That's exactly what it does. TouchID interfaces with the A#X chip on the iPhone. link

Right. For now...

But, why defend them bricking phones. Disable the touch id, don't brick the phone.

Its not that simple. The fingerprint scanner isn't just on a whitelist, it is cryptographically verified. If a person could bypass that, they could install a device that interfaces with the Apple A#X chip. From there, they could attempt to brute force the fingerprint.

The fingerprint itself is not stored on the reader. Instead, the biometric data is run through a secret algorithm that produces a value stored on the A#X chip. If the fingerprint reader and the chip produce matching values, the challenge is passed. It is highly likely that this algorithm does not produce unique outputs, and a clever mutation algorithm could quickly produce a match.

In short, Apple is throwing up barriers to people that would steal your phone and your data. This has the distinct side effect of killing the stolen phone market, which I'm all for.

What I'm saying is, force them to use passcode if the touch id isn't something Apple can trust.

Short version is: Finger -> Touch ID/Passcode -> Unlock If touch id is compromised: Finger -> Passcode only -> Unlock

Doing it without warning is a terrible way to do it, and I don't see how that can be defended.
